title: Min-CSP approximation at the SDP integrality gap
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal:
For every fixed finite domain \(D\), positive arity \(k\), and finite set \(\Lambda\) of nonnegative rational cost functions \(f:D^k\to[0,1]\), is the following true? For every rational \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a randomized polynomial-time algorithm which, on every \(n\)-variable minimization \(\Lambda\)-CSP instance \(I\) with finite \(n\)-variable SDP integrality gap \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\), returns an assignment \(\sigma\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)\leq (1+\varepsilon)\alpha_\Lambda(n)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\bigr]\geq\tfrac23?\]
The same algorithm handles all \(n\); it also halts and returns an assignment on the sizes where the gap is infinite, but no multiplicative guarantee is imposed there. The gap and the basic SDP are defined below.
why: A universal theorem would extend the general SDP approximation framework to multiplicative minimization guarantees, including instances whose optimum vanishes with input size. It would connect a geometric obstruction of a standard relaxation to actual polynomial-time approximation across all finite cost languages. A counterexample would identify a limit to interpreting integrality gaps as achievable algorithmic benchmarks.
status_note: The 2017 chapter explicitly poses this n-dependent multiplicative question after distinguishing it from the 2009 additive rounding theorem. The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper supplies results under additional template hypotheses, not the universal statement. A bounded primary-source search checked on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this does not establish that the historical question remains open beyond the checked sources.

progress.text: Raghavendra and Steurer prove a universal rounding result for the integrality-gap curve, with additive accuracy losses.
Makarychev and Makarychev explain why the additive theorem does not give the corresponding minimization ratio, then pose the n-dependent multiplicative question as Open Problem 4.
New robust-satisfiability guarantees are proved under specified algebraic preservation hypotheses; they provide special-family progress rather than a matching theorem for every finite cost language.

importance.reason: A universal bridge between SDP integrality gaps and polynomial-time multiplicative approximation would organize minimization across all finite-domain cost languages, including near-satisfiable instances where the existing additive theory loses its guarantee.
importance.basis: Individual source and scope review of the universal n-dependent gap question; significance is editorial, not a proof-status judgment.

sentences: A minimization CSP assigns finite-domain values to variables to minimize the average of fixed local nonnegative costs.
Its basic SDP can achieve a lower cost using consistent local distributions and vectors than any actual assignment.
The question asks whether a randomized polynomial-time algorithm can match the SDP’s worst gap at each number of variables within every factor 1+ε.
The multiplicative guarantee must also protect zero or very small optimum values, which existing additive universal rounding does not do.
A resolution would clarify whether size-dependent SDP gaps universally predict achievable approximation for minimization CSPs.

definitions:
Fix \(D=\{1,\ldots,q\}\), with \(q\geq1\), and a finite nonempty \(\Lambda\). Its rational cost tables and \(k\geq1\) are fixed, not input. The nonnegative rational convention gives a finite effective version of the source’s generalized nonnegative predicates; negative costs do not define the multiplicative approximation question. An instance has variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), \(n\geq1\), and a finite list of \(m\) constraints \(C=(f_C,(i_1,\ldots,i_k))\). Every \(f_C\in\Lambda\), and each \(i_j\in[n]\). Repeated coordinates and repeated occurrences are allowed, with each occurrence having unit weight. There are no hard constraints, infinite costs, extra unary pins or input-dependent predicates. For an assignment \(\sigma:[n]\to D\), set
\[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)=\frac1m\sum_C f_C(\sigma(i_1),\ldots,\sigma(i_k)),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_\sigma\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma).\]
For \(m=0\), cost and optimum are zero. A zero-one cost table records violation by value one and satisfaction by value zero. Different arities can be represented by a common maximum arity with unused arguments; the question is not restricted to Boolean predicates.

Define the basic semidefinite relaxation as follows. Choose real vectors \(v_0,u_{i,a}\in\mathbb R^{1+nq}\), for \(i\in[n],a\in D\), satisfying
\[\langle v_0,v_0\rangle=1,\qquad \sum_{a\in D}u_{i,a}=v_0,\qquad \langle u_{i,a},u_{i,b}\rangle=0\quad(a\ne b).\]
For each constraint occurrence \(C\), let \(S_C\) be its set of distinct variables and choose a local distribution \(\mu_C:D^{S_C}\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) with total mass one. Impose
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{i,a}\rangle\quad(i\in S_C),\]
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a,\ z(j)=b}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{j,b}\rangle\quad(i,j\in S_C,\ i\ne j).\]
Thus all local one- and two-variable marginals agree with the common vector inner products. Repeated occurrences of a variable in a constraint use the same value \(z(i)\). The SDP value \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) is the minimum of
\[\frac1m\sum_C\sum_{z\in D^{S_C}}\mu_C(z)f_C(z(i_1),\ldots,z(i_k)),\]
with value zero when \(m=0\). This is a finite semidefinite program via its Gram matrix; the stated vector dimension suffices for every such matrix. It is feasible and compact in Gram-matrix and distribution coordinates. Every assignment gives a feasible point, so \(0\leq\operatorname{SDP}(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). No higher level of an SDP hierarchy is included.

For a fixed instance define its gap ratio as \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) if the denominator is positive, as one if both values are zero, and as \(+\infty\) if only the denominator is zero. Let \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\) be the supremum of these ratios over all lists of constraints on exactly \(n\) labelled variables; unused variables are counted. Then \(1\leq\alpha_\Lambda(n)\leq+\infty\), and the gap may grow with \(n\). The algorithm is not supplied with its value or an oracle for it. This is an instance-size gap, not a single constant supremum over every size.

Encode \(n,m\) in unary and each constraint by its fixed-table index and its \(k\) variable indices in binary; the total bit length is \(L\). The algorithm is a finite probabilistic multitape Turing machine using independent fair coin bits. For each fixed \(D,k,\Lambda,\varepsilon\), one program has worst-case running time \(C(L+1)^c\) on every input and every coin sequence; \(C,c\) may depend on these fixed parameters. Malformed strings may be rejected. The output explicitly gives all \(n\) labels. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), common exponent across languages or effective algorithm for finding the program from \(\Lambda\) is required. The probability convention is the explicit bounded-error interpretation of the source’s randomized approximation framework.

The guarantee is multiplicative, relative to the actual optimum. When that optimum is zero and the size-dependent gap is finite, the algorithm must find a zero-cost assignment with probability at least \(2/3\). There is no additive error term, and no assertion that it must round a supplied SDP point or achieve the stronger bound with \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) in place of \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal algorithmic assertion, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must establish one polynomial-time machine for every fixed language and positive accuracy, working at all input sizes with the stated success probability, size-dependent gap and zero-optimum convention. A negative proof must establish a fixed finite language and positive accuracy for which no such machine exists. A constant additive guarantee for normalized cost, an algorithm restricted to one predicate family, or a conditional obstruction to one rounding scheme does not settle the universal statement. An unproved complexity assumption may support partial progress but is not part of this unconditional target.

source_formulation.text: If the minimization SDP gap at n variables is α_n, can a polynomial-time algorithm attain approximation factor (1+ε)α_n for every positive ε?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Chapter 11, §7, Open Problem 4; the n-dependent gap is retained, with finite cost encoding, zero cases and success probability made explicit.

context_blocks.text: The integrality gap measures a relaxation’s worst discrepancy from a genuine assignment. In minimization, the SDP can make local constraints appear cheaper than any global assignment. This question asks whether an efficient algorithm can always match the resulting size-dependent benchmark to arbitrarily small relative slack; it does not ask to compute the gap itself.

The source distinguishes maximization and minimization with nonnegative predicates. For maximization, a random assignment provides a positive baseline for each nonzero fixed predicate, allowing additive approximation losses to become relative losses. For minimization, satisfiable or nearly satisfiable instances can have optimum zero or arbitrarily close to zero, so the same argument fails.

Raghavendra and Steurer’s universal rounding theorem obtains the integrality-gap curve with an additive error in both its argument and its returned objective. Its running-time dependence on that additive accuracy can be very large. Taking the accuracy to shrink with the instance size therefore does not yield the polynomial-time multiplicative guarantee asked here.

The source explicitly permits α_n to depend on n. Replacing it by one global constant would discard major minimization examples, while a generic additive approximation to a normalized objective would leave zero and very small costs unprotected. These are essential parts of the question, not presentation choices.

The 2026 robust-satisfiability work obtains quantitative guarantees for specified majority and plurality preservation classes, along with separate conditional hardness for a particular promise problem. Those results concern selected families and loss curves. They do not assert a universal algorithm matching the exact n-variable multiplicative SDP gap for every finite nonnegative cost language.
